Title: Montague's 2026 Wildcat Salute takes on new meaning because of 9-11
Article_Text:
MONTAGUE — The 2026 Wildcat Salute took on added meaning when it was held Sept. 11, 25 years after terrorists attacked the World Trade Center and Pentagon using hijacked airliners.
A fourth hijacked plane crashed in a Pennsylvania field after passengers and crew members attempted to regain control of the aircraft.
The annual event at Montague High School’s football field involved much more than the football game, in which the Wildcats defeated Oakridge 34-28.
The evening included military and first responder displays, aircraft, awards and quilts honoring veterans and others who have served their communities.
Event coordinator Jacquie Wood, a retired Montague teacher, said organizing the event began with securing the Hooligans Flight Team for an aerial appearance.
“It’s always a lot of work,” Wood said. “First, we have to secure the airplanes — the Hooligans — and they had other people wanting them, especially because it was 9/11, so I secured them early.”
Wood said Mona Shores delayed its game so the Hooligans could appear at the Wildcat Salute first.
She also arranged for a parachutist and contacted representatives of the military branches. Because the event was held on Sept. 11, however, some equipment and personnel were unavailable.
“We couldn’t get the Coast Guard boat, and we couldn’t get some of the big tactical vehicles we have had here,” Wood said. “We got some, but not all of them.”
Representatives of several military branches and local first responder agencies attended.
Among those recognized was Marine Corps veteran Sgt. John P. Casazza. He received a commemorative Purple Heart plaque created and presented by Doug Pickel, with Mike Baauw, a department manager and veterans service officer with Muskegon County Veterans Affairs, participating in the ceremony.
According to information provided for the ceremony, Casazza served with the 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines in Vietnam from 1967 to 1968. He participated in 10 major operations, including fighting at Hue City during the Tet Offensive.
Casazza served as a machine gunner and machine gun squad leader and was a platoon sergeant during the Tet Offensive. His decorations include the Purple Heart, Bronze Star Medal with “V” device, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, Republic of Vietnam Campaign Medal, Combat Action Ribbon, Presidential Unit Citation and Good Conduct Medal.
The presentation also recognized Casazza’s family connection to the Sept. 11 attacks.
His sister, Ann Hawksby, was working on the 57th floor of the World Trade Center’s South Tower. She was running down the stairs when the second hijacked plane struck the tower near the floor where she had worked.
Hawksby escaped after losing a shoe and leaving her telephone behind. Many people from her office were killed, according to the narrative read during the ceremony. The experience was so traumatic that she was unable to return to New York City.
Casazza’s nephew, John Francis Casazza, 38, was killed in the North Tower. He was a senior vice president and government bonds trader for Cantor Fitzgerald and worked on the 104th floor, above where the first plane struck.
According to the family’s account, he called his wife, Patti, several times and said he intended to reach the roof, but the doors were locked. The tower collapsed soon afterward. A small amount of his remains was identified through DNA testing two years later.
Casazza also received a 25th anniversary Sept. 11 memorial award bearing the message, “We will never forget.”
Another Montague graduate, Army veteran Gregory Charles Dahl, received a Michigan Vietnam Veteran Award created by Pickel and presented by Baauw.
The recognition honors Michigan veterans who served in the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, Air Force and Coast Guard during the Vietnam War era.
Dahl served in the Army from 1972 to 1973 as a military police officer. His decorations include the National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, Republic of Vietnam Campaign Medal with 1960 device, Meritorious Unit Commendation and marksmanship qualification badges for the M16 rifle and .45-caliber pistol.
According to information provided for the ceremony, Dahl was drafted around the time he graduated from Montague High School in 1971. He completed training at Fort Benning, Georgia, and received clearance to handle classified material.
Dahl was assigned to Ramasun Station in Thailand, where a large antenna system known as the “Elephant Cage” intercepted radio communications. Intelligence gathered at the installation was passed to U.S. military forces.
Dahl worked 12-hour shifts and encountered wild dogs, scorpions, spiders and venomous snakes. Personnel had to inspect their boots before putting them on. Dahl also received treatment for a toxic exposure, according to the ceremony narrative.
The narrative said people sometimes attempted to smuggle items onto the installation aboard garbage trucks and other vehicles. Dahl and other guards also encountered intoxicated residents who threw snakes at them.
“The best part of his service was when he was able to come home to the country he loves,” the ceremony narrative stated.
Dahl continues to serve with the honor guard at VFW Post 3256.
Retired Montague Fire Chief Ron Anderson received a 25th anniversary Sept. 11 fire department award recognizing his service to the community.
The award, created by Pickel, was presented by Jonathon Degen and members of the Montague Fire Department. The program identified Degen as the department’s current chief.
According to the recognition read during the ceremony, Anderson served the department for more than 40 years, including a period as fire chief. The citation credited him with mentoring generations of firefighters and guiding the department through numerous emergencies and challenges.
Although Anderson recently stepped down as chief, the program said he continues to serve as an active member of the department.
The citation described Anderson as a hometown hero whose leadership and commitment earned the respect of fellow firefighters and community members.
Montague police officer Ryan Rought received a 25th anniversary Sept. 11 police department award.
The award, created by Pickel, was presented by Montague Police Chief Rick Johnson and members of the Police Department. The city identifies Rought as a part-time officer.
Nancy Frye was among the other people honored during the event. Her husband, Hugh Frye, accompanied her.
Nancy Frye received two awards, including one she described as a medal presented by Native Americans. She said she was the only woman to receive it. She also was recognized as a Hometown Hero for her involvement in the community and politics.
“To be with all the veterans who are here and were honored, it was a gift,” she said.
Nancy Frye served four years of active duty in the Air Force. Hugh Frye served for 23 years as an Air Force military police officer. The couple met while serving in the military and later married.
“We’ve been coming here for a long time,” Hugh Frye said. “She was getting an award tonight, and I especially wanted to be here.”
Air Force recruiter Travis Spears also attended.
“I’m here to watch some really good football, help bring some life to the Air Force and represent all veterans who have served in the Air Force,” Spears said.
Spears recruits in Muskegon, Grand Haven and Spring Lake and also travels to the Ludington area.
“I hope to help people figure out what they want to do after high school and give people who don’t have a direction in their lives another opportunity,” he said.
Another attraction was the arrival of a Michigan State Police helicopter, which landed in the outfield of the Wildcats’ baseball field.
“We were requested by the event hosts to come and be part of the event,” MSP Sgt. Mike Murray said.
Murray said the helicopter is used for search-and-rescue missions and appears at large community events to promote law enforcement and recruitment.
Montague Fire Department and White Lake Ambulance personnel also attended with a fire engine and rescue vehicle.
“We’re here to support the Montague Wildcats and to represent the 9/11 victims,” Degen said.
Degen said the vehicles were displayed so children could see the equipment and learn about the Montague Fire Department. Although the department was not conducting a formal recruitment effort during the event, he said it is always looking for people interested in joining.

Title: This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms

YARDLEY, Pa. – Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing.
But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party's congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.
Recommended Videos
Until now.
This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.
Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that “I don't see it happening.”
Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick’s reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump’s recent midterm convention in Dallas.
But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president’s sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.
Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year's political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote.
“That’s the job,” he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview.
Democrats have tried for years to defeat Fitzpatrick
Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms.
“The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for,” he said in an interview this summer. “I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation.”
Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points.
“Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway,” said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. “It’s, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time.”
Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick.
“I’m not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that’s very, very different than any race he’s ever run before,” he said.
Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump's immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party's leaders.
“He's a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community,” she said. But, she added, “you have to serve everyone in your district."
Fitzpatrick has been willing to criticize Trump
Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020.
Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.
“You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart,” Rachau said.
In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV “weak,” and captive to the “Radical Left."
“There’s so many angry voices out there. We all know that's the case,” Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. “People are sick and tired of the noise. They’re sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about.”
Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church's parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.
Fitzpatrick spends millions on attack ads against Harvie
Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.
According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged.
The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.
No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker’s lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other.
Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president.
“Incumbents just feel they can’t cross that line. If they do, they’re not going to get reelected," she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. "They might not get reelected anyway.”

Title: Ed Sheeran is set to return to stage for 1st time since Macklemore was cut and other acts withdrew
Article_Text:
PHILADELPHIA – Ed Sheeran is set to resume his tour Saturday — possibly solo — after all his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.
It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original U.S. opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.
Recommended Videos
Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.
Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists' support. As of Saturday afternoon, tickets were still available for the show, and his website did not list any replacement acts.
A group of about 50 pro-Palestinian demonstrators rallied outside the stadium. Rose Tejada, 20, of Philadelphia, expressed disappointment that Sheeran did not take a stand on the issue.
“This is endemic in Western culture that we believe we can stay out of conflict, be apolitical,” Tejada said.
The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey. Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday.
Within hours of Sheeran's statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.
Jessica Grono, 51, planned to drive 30 minutes from her Phoenixville home to attend the concert. She has liked Sheeran since his song “The A Team” was released in 2011 and loves his voice, music and storytelling.
“I feel bad for him,” Grono said, adding that he has not said anything wrong and should not be penalized for others’ words.
Macklemore said Wednesday he is donating $1 million to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift; a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million but have not specified where the money will be directed. Sheeran's representatives have not responded to multiple requests for comment.
Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the No. 3 top-earning concert act since 2021.
Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.
The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.
He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.
While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran's magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.
___
Associated Press journalist Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed.

Title: Ed Sheeran concert ticket prices plummet as pro-Palestine protests planned amid Macklemore controversy
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran concert ticket prices plummet as pro-Palestine protests planned amid Macklemore controversy
Ed Sheeran's The Loop tour is set to continue in the US on Saturday, with pro-Palestine protests also planned outside the venue as all support acts have withdrawn from the remaining dates
Pro-Palestine demonstrations are being planned outside the US venue where Ed Sheeran is set to perform on Saturday, as tickets for the concerts are now on sale for as little as $76 (€88).
This week, all of the support acts for the singer's ongoing The Loop tour announced they were pulling out of the remaining dates after Macklemore, real name Benjamin Haggerty, was dropped from the line-up over remarks he made regarding Gaza.
Sheeran's own backing band, Irish act Beoga, also confirmed they were withdrawing, writing in a statement on Instagram that they "fully supported" Macklemore's message.
The 35-year-old English singer launched his tour in Auckland, New Zealand, in January.
It is due to conclude in Mexico City in December, with a total of 18 shows still scheduled across North and South America.
Sheeran is next due to take to the stage in Philadelphia on Saturday evening, with tickets currently on sale for as little as $76 (€88).
Ahead of that performance, local pro-Palestinian groups have announced they will be staging protests outside the venue, Lincoln Financial Field, reports the Mirror.
In a post shared on Instagram, the Philly Palestine Coalition and Shut Down Dand outlined plans to "take to the streets to return the conversation to Palestine, and return Philadelphia to action".
The minimum ticket price for his following concert in Foxborough, Massachusetts, on September 25, rises to $112 (€130).
While Sheeran's two performances in Hollywood, Florida, on October 29 and 30, currently advertise minimum ticket prices of $339 US dollars (€395), prices drop once more for his final show in Tampa on November 7.
Tickets for that particular show are available from a minimum of €87 US dollars (€101). For his closing performance of the tour in Mexico City, prices currently begin at 3,550 pesos, or €179.
Among the acts who have withdrawn from Sheeran's tour are Irish singer Aaron Rowe, Grammy award-winning artist Finneas, brother of Billie Eilish, and Danish singer Lukas Graham.
On Monday, Macklemore took to Instagram claiming Sheeran and his team had "made the decision to remove" him from the Loop Tour.
In a response posted on the platform on Tuesday, Sheeran maintained that his departure from the tour was the promoter's call and not his own.
He stated that "upcoming tour dates had communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting", adding that Robert Kraft, owner of Gillette Stadium, where he had been scheduled to perform, was amongst them.
Sheeran continued: "I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own personal way."
The Shape Of You hitmaker said he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", adding that he respected Macklemore "as an artist".

Title: Eagles-Titans: Drew Brees to call first Birds game, who haven't been great in Nashville
Article_Text:
Eagles-Titans: Hall of Famer Drew Brees to call first Birds game in second chance with Fox
Brees is still a work in progress but has improved as a broadcaster alongside Adam Amin, who has a knack for helping former stars.
The Philadelphia Eagles (1-0) are on the road this week to take on the Tennessee Titans (0-1), and a Hall of Fame quarterback is joining them in Nashville.
Drew Brees, the Super Bowl XLIV MVP who spent 20 seasons in the NFL, will be in the booth to call the game on Fox alongside play-by-play partner Adam Amin. Kristina Pink will report from the sidelines of Nissan Stadium.
Similar to his playing career, Brees has been forced to overcome adversity as a broadcaster. He was hired by NBC in 2020 and appeared to be on track to replace Cris Collinsworth on Sunday Night Football, but a widely criticized performance in his first NFL broadcast — a 2021 wild-card game — led to his departure from the network.
“When Drew shows up in the booth, who wouldn’t want to listen to him?” Fox Sports’ president and executive producer Brad Zager told Sports Business Journal before the start of the season. “You saw with Tom [Brady] that he had 18 weeks of reps with an ‘A’ crew his first year, and you saw that improvement. Drew never really had that on the NFL level. He does that playoff game, and everybody has their opinions.”
Fox turned to Brees last season to replace former Eagles quarterback Mark Sanchez, who was fired following a late-night fight in October where he allegedly attacked and stabbed a delivery driver. Brees has now called nine game in the network’s No. 3 booth alongside Amin, who has been impressed by the Hall of Famer’s deep understanding of the game and the gravitas he brings to the booth.
It was certainly on display last week when the pair called the Chicago Bears’ 59-37 drubbing of the Carolina Panthers. Bears quarterback Caleb Williams credited advice Brees offered during a production meeting before the game with helping him focus on sticking with his reads and not overlooking open targets in search of a big play.
“We want to encourage him to use his voice and take [viewers] another layer deeper,” Amin said. “And I think he’s starting to improve as a presenter. He still has to learn some of the timing and rhythm, but a lot of that just comes with doing the job. And the rest of it, the presentation, is going to come with timing and confidence.”
In a way, Brees is fortunate to have been paired with Amin, who is in his seventh season with Fox and has a track record of working with recently retired players. That includes Sanchez on the football side and Adam Wainwright and A.J. Pierzynski on MLB games. Despite working with former All-Stars and MVPs, Amin has found most of his on-air partners to be coachable, and Brees has been no exception.
“Most people don’t get a lot of coaching or guidance when they first step into the booth,” Amin said. “I have a process. I know what the feel of the broadcast looks and feels like and what the timing and rhythm of it is. And I go, ‘Man, here’s the timing and rhythm that I work off of. Let’s start there.’”
“It’s funny to listen to him use television terminology,” Amin added. “Like, ‘Hey, let’s talk about this graphic’ or ‘Hey, what does the viz do?’ It’s like learning a new playbook for him.”
As for Sunday’s game, one thing Amin will be watching is how the Eagles offensive line deals with Titans star Jeffery Simmons, who appeared to take a shot at Jalen Hurts earlier this week.
“Simmons did not get a whole lot done against Landon Dickerson the last time they met in 2022,” Amin said. “Obviously, Dickerson is hurt, so who gets the assignment on Simmons?”
According to The Inquirer’s Jeff McLane, all indications point to the assignment falling to Drew Kendall in what would be his first career start.
“The All-Pro lines up at multiple spots inside, but it’s likely Titans coach Robert Saleh will concentrate his efforts vs. Kendall,” McLane wrote.
How to watch and stream Eagles vs. Titans
Sunday’s Week 2 game between the Eagles and Titans is scheduled to start at 1 p.m. Philadelphia time on Fox.
The game will stream on Fox One, the network’s subscription streaming service. It’s also available on any so-called skinny bundle that carries Fox, including fuboTV, YouTube TV, Hulu + Live TV, Sling TV, and DirecTV Stream. Most offer a free trial.
If you live in Philadelphia or any other TV market where the game is airing, you can also stream the game on NFL+, the league’s subscription streaming service, which runs $6.99 a month.
If you’re looking to stream the game for free and you live in or around Philadelphia, your best option is to use a digital antenna, since the game will air on broadcast television on Fox 29.
The game can also be heard on 94.1 WIP, with Merrill Reese — in his 50th season as the voice of the Eagles — calling the game alongside former Birds receiver Mike Quick.
Live Eagles coverage from The Inquirer
Staff writers Jeff McLane, Olivia Reiner, Jeff Neiburg, and Ryan Novozinsky will be covering the action live on Inquirer.com.
Notes and observations about the game can be found at Inquirer.com/Eagles. Don’t forget to subscribe to our free Sports Daily newsletter.
The Eagles haven’t had much success in Nashville
Sunday’s matchup is just the fourth time the Eagles have traveled to Nashville to face the Titans since the franchise moved to Nissan Stadium in 1999.
Overall, the Eagles are 8-5 against the Titans, but they haven’t had much success down in the Music City, losing all three games they’ve played there. The most recent was an overtime loss to the Titans in 2018, when Carson Wentz was quarterback and Nelson Agholor — who recently joined NFL Media as an analyst — was still dropping passes.
The last time the two teams played was in Week 12 of the 2022 season, with the Birds dominating the Titans in a 35-10 win in something of a revenge game for former Eagles wide receiver A.J. Brown.

Title: Eagles vs. Titans: Week 2 predictions, odds, injury updates, and more
Article_Text:
Eagles vs. Titans: Predictions, odds, injury updates, and why everyone is talking about the weather in Week 2
The Eagles aren’t just facing the Titans on Sunday. According to Jordan Davis, there’s a potential “second opponent” they need to watch out for: the heat. Here’s what you need to know.
Jordan Davis didn’t think for very long before offering an answer to the hottest football game he has ever played in.
“It has to be Tampa two years ago,” Davis said Friday.
The Eagles, in their last game before an early Week 5 bye that changed the trajectory of their Super Bowl season, were dominated by the Bucs, 33-16, in a game that wasn’t even that close. The real feel on the field reached triple digits.
Davis, who is from North Carolina and played his college football at Georgia and all across the American South, knew he was in for a long day long before the game started.
“It’s when you’re walking out, the warmup before the warmup, and you’re already sweating in like two minutes,” he said. “You didn’t even finish stretching yet, and you’re dripping.
“I don’t like that feeling.”
He won’t be able to avoid it Sunday. The Eagles and Titans play in Nashville at noon local time, and the city is under a heat advisory. Temperatures are expected to be in the mid-90s, and the feel on the field could reach triple digits, just like it did in Tampa, Fla., each of the last two years.
Nick Sirianni studies everything his team does, down to travel times and all that goes into a trip. The Eagles had another early-season game in Tampa last year, and they took their data from 2024 and left a day earlier to try to acclimate. Sirianni doesn’t like to be entirely results-oriented, but the Eagles left Florida with a 31-25 victory.
That’s in part why they left for Tennessee on Friday evening.
“It benefited us,” Sirianni said of leaving early last year, “and that’s why we decided to do that again.”
What are some of the worst parts about playing in extreme heat?
“It kind of slows your cognitive ability,” Davis said. “You can’t think as fast. You’re just kind of fighting for survival and also playing a football game at the same time if you really feel it.
“You really have a second opponent if you’re not careful.”
Mind over matter, right?
“It’s mind over matter until your body is cramping up and locking up,” center Cam Jurgens said. “Then you’re like, ‘Well it’s a little bit of matter now.’”

Final injury report
The Eagles again will be without top edge rusher Jonathan Greenard, who continues to practice in a limited capacity but is not ready to play as he recovers from a pectoral injury.
“I feel like they’ve done a great job here with the rehab process,” Greenard said Thursday. “I’m feeling better. I’m getting more and more confident in it and just only going to stack days to where I can eventually get out there.”

Storylines to watch
The biggest takeaway from last week’s 24-22 win over Washington probably was the offensive line’s inability to consistently protect Jalen Hurts from pressure and create lanes for Saquon Barkley.
The line will look different Sunday in Nashville. The Eagles have been keeping Landon Dickerson’s replacement close to the vest, but it’s expected to be Drew Kendall. Could this be addition by subtraction for the Eagles? We’ll find out Sunday.
Elsewhere on offense, Makai Lemon’s first real NFL game went about as well as his first preseason game. It’s way too early to be alarmed by Lemon’s usage and production, but the Eagles are going to need more from their first-round pick if the offense wants to be more dynamic. Lemon knows he has “lots to improve on” moving forward.
- Could Hollywood Brown get more involved this week? The receiver Howie Roseman signed to a deal worth $5 million in guaranteed money didn’t see the field in Week 1 and was surprised by it.
- Jalen Carter and Cooper DeJean sat out on Wednesday, the first practice day of the week, before returning Thursday. Both are set to go Sunday, but Carter was sporting a cast on his right wrist.
- DeJean, meanwhile, is looking to bounce back from a Week 1 performance he said “wasn’t good enough.”
Our Eagles Week 2 preview show
I said that and more on this week’s Gameday Central preview show with my beat partner Olivia Reiner. Watch our full Week 2 show here.

Eagles-Titans predictions

Ryan Novozinsky: Eagles 28, Titans 13
You can also check out the reasoning behind our picks and McLane’s keys to the game. As for the rest of the country, here’s a look at the national media predictions for Sunday.
One number to know
176
Jalen Hurts threw for 203 yards in Week 1, and 176 of them came on throws that traveled at least 10 air yards, according to Next Gen Stats, which counts any throw of 10 or more air yards as a “downfield” pass.
Hurts completed six of his nine downfield attempts and the Eagles scored all three of their touchdowns that way.
The Titans were susceptible to the deep ball last year and that carried over into Week 1.
There are other numbers working in the Eagles’ favor, too.
Latest Week 2 odds
The Eagles are favored by a touchdown in their road game Sunday in Nashville, a number that has held steady at most sportsbooks throughout the week.
The over/under for the game, 39½, is the lowest of the 16 Week 2 NFL games.
As for what oddsmakers think about Hurts’ ability to throw against a Tennessee defense that isn’t all that strong? They don’t expect Hurts to throw for a whole lot more than he did against Washington.
What we’re saying about the Eagles
Here’s what our columnists are saying this week, starting with David Murphy, who ponders if “expecting a 40-spot is really too much to ask?”
David Murphy: “Every week, Nick Sirianni reminds us that winning is hard in the National Football League. Every victory is like a delicate child, something to nurture and cherish. … But, please, convince us. Forget all of that mumbo jumbo about a win being a win on any given Sunday. Wins are great. They’re much better when you feel good about them.” Read more.
Mike Sielski: “You ask why Landon Dickerson played against the Commanders, why in doing so he basically dared coach Nick Sirianni to make the difficult decision to bench him, why he was willing to damage the cohesion and performance of the Eagles’ offensive line, and the question answers itself. Next man up is a convenient cliche. Too many people forget or don’t give a damn about its corollary: First man, out. Sometimes for good.” Read more.
Murphy: “Two plays from Sunday illustrate the blurry line between results and reality. Both involve Makai Lemon, the rookie wide receiver who is currently threatening the integrity of the space-time continuum with a career average of minus-1.7 yards per reception on three catches.” Read more.
What the Titans are saying
Titans star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons certainly provided some bulletin board material earlier in the week when he said the Titans “just need to make Jalen Hurts be a QB.”
Perhaps he didn’t mean it as a slight, but the reaction to Simmons’ comments took it as one.
Eagles left tackle and captain Jordan Mailata, though, didn’t take the bait.
“I don’t see them,” Mailata said when asked about Simmons’ comments. “I don’t pay attention to that stuff. That’s clickbait stuff. That’s what you guys get paid for, you guys that promote that stuff.
“He can say it. You guys don’t need to say it to me. That’s all I know. I don’t listen to that stuff. I only care about everybody in this locker room. This locker room is the only thing I give a damn about. I don’t care what you guys say about this locker room, and I don’t care what any other locker room says about this locker room.”
Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll on playing the Eagles: “Coach Sirianni is an excellent head coach. 42-4 when he wins the turnover ratio, which is a pretty impressive stat. So that’s going to be paramount. Coach Fangio has done this for about 40 years in the NFL, plus whatever he did in college. Tremendous scheme, very sound. … And then, you add the players, a collection of players that Howie [Roseman] assembles each and every year. It’s a tough challenge.”
Hear more about what the Titans are saying heading into Sunday’s game.
What the national media is saying
How bad were the Titans in Week 1? Here’s what ESPN’s Ben Solak had to say earlier in the week:
“I cannot remember a team that looked less functional on offense in Week 1 than the Titans in Sunday’s loss to the Jets. I went back and looked at the past few seasons of Week 1 travesties — Russell Wilson’s Giants had six points in 2025; Daniel Jones’ Giants had six points in 2024; Jones’ Giants also had zero points in 2023; oh my goodness, are all of these just Giants games? — and I still don’t remember seeing something I found this particularly problematic.
“The Titans looked as if they had never played together before.”
Yikes.
Jason Kelce on Dallas Goedert: “This offense I think will fit [Goedert] pretty well,” Kelce said. “All this misdirection and stuff, they scheme things up, and it stresses those linebackers.”

Title: Seven MLB Players and Managers Facing Pressure Down the Stretch
Article_Text:
Seven MLB Players and Managers Facing Pressure Down the Stretch
In this story:
The stretch run of the MLB regular season is well upon us, with just over a week left before playoff baseball begins. Races are coming down to the wire and pressure is building across the league.
For some players and managers, the final weeks of the season could define how their years are remembered. Some are trying to lift their teams to the postseason, while others are fighting to solidify their roles in October. Jobs could be on the line.
With only a short time left to change how their seasons end, the following seven MLB figures are under the most pressure and have the most at stake down the stretch.
Editor’s note: All stats are updated through Thursday’s games.
Gerrit Cole, Yankees SP
The Yankees remain one of the favorites in the American League and that’s largely due to their elite pitching staff. New York leads MLB in ERA (3.19) by a wide margin, and the starting rotation also tops the competition with a 3.26 ERA. Gerrit Cole was once the ace of the staff, but there are questions as to where he’ll fit in October given his shaky performances of late and how good the rest of the rotation has been.
After missing all of 2025, Cole returned from Tommy John surgery on May 22 and has endured an up-and-down season. Entering Friday’s matchup against the Diamondbacks, he’s 8–9 with a 3.67 ERA, 1.13 WHIP and 117 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings. The concerning part is that in his last two starts, against the Padres and Mets, he’s allowed seven home runs in 11 ⅓ innings. His September ERA has ballooned to 6.48 in three starts as a result.
Cam Schlittler has been the best pitcher in the American League this season and should be the Yankees’ Game 1 starter in the postseason. Veteran Max Fried isn’t far behind and has his own argument to make given his track record and 2.63 ERA this season. Carlos Rodón (6–3, 2.95 ERA) could slot in above Cole at No. 3, given their recent performances, which may leave Cole off the Yankees’ roster for a three-game wild-card series.
After Friday’s start against Arizona, Cole has just one start left in the regular season. He’ll be under tremendous pressure to prove he deserves a guaranteed start in the postseason.
Manny Machado, Padres 3B
Machado is the de facto captain of the Padres and, along with Fernando Tatis Jr., is the face of the franchise. With San Diego holding a four-game lead over the Diamondbacks for the NL’s final wild-card spot entering the season’s penultimate weekend, if the team misses the playoffs he’ll shoulder a large percentage of the blame, given his status and how poorly he was hitting early in the year.
Through June 30, Machado was having his worst professional season. He was slashing .189/.274/.399 with 16 home runs, 46 RBIs and a wRC+ of 86. It was a brutal showing for a guy counting $31.8 million against the luxury tax payroll. In the 61 games since, he’s slashed .257/.349/.427 with 12 homers, 39 RBIs and a wRC+ of 119, just a couple of points below his career average.
He’s looking more like himself at the right time but, fair or not, he has garnered a reputation for not coming through in big games. Machado owns a career .682 postseason OPS and was 1-for-10 with three strikeouts in San Diego’s brief postseason appearance last year. He needs to reverse that trend and get hot down the stretch.
Don Mattingly, Phillies manager
Mattingly took over as the interim manager of the Phillies on April 28 after the team started the year 9–19. Since then, Philadelphia has gone 74–49 in one of the more stark turnarounds we’ve seen in recent years. There's still more work to be done, though.
The Phillies are regarded as owning one of baseball’s strongest home-field advantages in the playoffs, and enter the weekend tied with the Cubs for the top wild-card spot and the right to host a wild-card series. Playing well enough down the stretch to outpace Chicago—and San Diego, who lurk just behind both teams—would do wonders for Philadelphia’s chance at advancing to the NLDS.
Rumors persist that the Phillies will move to hire Alex Cora as their manager this offseason, but Mattingly could force the team’s hand with a strong finish. If the franchise is set on Cora, Mattingly needs to change their mind. Limping to the line is not the way to do that.
Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Blue Jays 1B
The Blue Jays are somehow still in contention for the AL’s final wild-card spot despite a litany of injuries and their star player enduring the worst season of his careerf. After a remarkable postseason in 2025, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has been playing like the Monstars sapped his power. With his team fighting for a playoff spot, the spotlight will be on the 27-year-old over the next few weeks.
Through 138 games, Guerrero is slashing .262/.334/.360 with just nine home runs, 56 RBIs and a career-low wRC+ of 97. His slugging percentage is a career low by more than 70 points, his on-base percentage is almost 50 points lower than his 2025 mark and his OPS (.694) is nearly 100 points lower than his career worst mark. It took him until Sept. 13, Toronto’s 75th home game, to hit his first home run at Rogers Centre this season. For reference, he hit home runs in each of the Blue Jays’ first two home games in the playoffs last year.
Toronto entered the season with World Series aspirations after falling short in seven games to the Dodgers last year. The team loaded up this offseason, expecting a big year. It has been a flop and, as their $500 million man, Guerrero is simultaneously the face of the franchise and the poster child for that failure. He has a few weeks to turn things around.
Joe Espada, Astros manager
Espada was the bench coach on Houston’s 2022 World Series-winning squad and was promoted to manager when Dusty Baker retired following the ’23 campaign. The results have not been great during his three seasons in charge.
The Astros won the AL West in 2024 with an 88–73 (.547) record. But they were swept by the Tigers in the wild-card series. In ’25, Houston missed the playoffs after going 87–75 due to losing a tiebreaker to Detroit. Astros owner Jim Crane feels that his team should be competing for titles on an annual basis, yet Espada’s teams have fell far short of those goals, and this year has been no different.
Houston has languished at or below .500 for most of the season yet somehow entered Friday with a one-game lead in the AL West. Missing the postseason for a second straight year would put Espada’s job in serious jeopardy. In fact, even if they make it, there’s a decent chance he’s gone without a deep run in the wake of GM Dana Brown’s firing last month.
José Ramírez, Guardians 3B
Like Guerrero, Ramírez is enduring one of the worst seasons of his career and, so far, the final month has not been kind to him. With the Guardians in a tight battle for both the AL Central and the wild card, Ramírez’s bat will be key if they hope to not only reach the postseason but do damage once they’re there.
In 117 games, Ramírez is slashing .230/.319/.364 with a 90 wRC+, all of those being his worst numbers since 2015. He only has 11 home runs, and his isolated power has dropped from .258 in 2024 to .134 this year.
Since undergoing surgery to repair a broken hamate bone in June, the 33-year-old has hit like a shell of himself. In 45 games since his return on July 22, Ramírez has posted a .567 OPS, and his slump has only deepened in September (.140 batting average, .345 OPS).
The cornerstone of Cleveland’s franchise is rounding third base of his prime years. We don’t know how many more shots he’ll get at a World Series.
Dan Wilson, Mariners manager
Like Espada and Mattingly, Wilson may be managing for his job the rest of the season.
After reaching the 2025 ALCS, Seattle returned much of the same roster but has seen very different results. Wilson has also given his critics plenty of ammo with his questionable bullpen management, which dates before this year. Mariners fans are still smarting after Wilson called on Eduardo Bazardo instead of closer Andrés Muñoz in a key moment of Game 7 of the ALCS, only for Bazardo to blow the lead. Following that, Seattle simply hasn’t played good baseball this year. The defense has been putrid as the Mariners rank dead last in Outs Above Average at -51.
A lot of Seattle’s issues simply come from key guys not playing up to their potential. Cal Raleigh is the biggest culprit, but Julio Rodríguez and Josh Naylor should also shoulder some of the blame. The Mariners are virtually assured of missing the playoffs—and have already clinched a losing record—but it is possible Wilson gets another year even if that happens. A strong finish would go a long way to securing that spot.

Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

Title: Phillies turn to improving Andrew Painter in clash vs. Mets
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 17:35 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Dale Zanine)
Christian Scott, Zac Thornton and Nolan McLean are providing the New York Mets hope that they eventually will be part of a rotation for a playoff contender.
The Philadelphia Phillies need rookie Andrew Painter to continue proving that now.
Painter will take the mound for the Phillies on Saturday afternoon when they visit the Mets in the third contest of a four-game series between the National League East rivals.
Painter (3-9, 5.54 ERA) will oppose Scott (4-5, 3.76) in a battle of right-handers.
The Phillies missed a chance to take over sole possession of the top wild-card spot in the NL on Friday night, when Thornton and two relievers combined on a six-hitter in the Mets' 6-3 win.
The Phillies, Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres are tied for the NL's three wild-card spots at 85-69. The Cubs lost to the Cincinnati Reds 6-4 before the Padres created the three-way tie hours later with an 8-2 win over the Miami Marlins.
The Arizona Diamondbacks reside five games behind the Phillies, Cubs and Padres.
The importance of Painter was further magnified Friday, when Philadelphia fell to 0-2 in bullpen games necessitated by the absence of left-hander Jesus Luzardo (shoulder, 15-day injured list).
The All-Star was scratched from his scheduled start against the Atlanta Braves last Saturday, when the Phillies used six pitchers as the Braves rolled to a 12-2 win. On Friday, opener Tim Mayza got just one out and allowed three runs while pitching in Luzardo's spot.
The Phillies' bullpen also is being taxed by injury and ineffectiveness.
Right-hander Jonathan Bowlan departed Thursday's game vs. the Mets with a tight right groin. On Friday, Orion Kerkering gave up Juan Soto's three-run blast in the sixth inning -- the second homer surrendered by Kerkering in his last three outings, during which he has a 13.50 ERA.
'Anybody that gives up runs, when things aren't going good, your confidence is not sky high like when you're getting all your outs and everything's going smoothly,' Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. 'But we've got to get past that at this point.'
Painter is 2-1 with a 3.58 ERA in nine starts since being recalled from Triple-A Lehigh Valley on July 31. He didn't factor into the decision in his most recent start last Sunday, when he gave up one run over five innings as the Phillies beat the Braves 9-4. He has yet to face the Mets in his career.
The Mets (70-84) have been under .500 since April and officially were eliminated from playoff contention earlier this week. But McLean and Thornton continued to provide optimism for 2027 by combining to allow just three runs over 12 innings in the first two games of the series.
McLean took the hard-luck loss Thursday, when he gave up one run in six innings in the Phillies' 3-0 win.
Thornton, McLean and Scott have a combined 3.40 ERA in 66 starts. Thornton and McLean are rookies while Scott is in his second big-league season after Tommy John surgery cut his 2024 campaign short.
'I think you have to train like you've never won anything and compete like you've never lost,' Mets interim manager Andy Green said Friday night about Thornton. 'I think you have to live in that space constantly.'
Scott took the defeat Sunday after allowing two runs over six innings in the Mets' 2-0 loss to the New York Yankees. He is 1-0 with a 1.80 ERA in two career starts against the Phillies.
--Field Level Media

Title: Carbon admin honored for 45 years – Times News Online
Article_Text:
Carbon admin honored for 45 years
Carbon County commissioners surprised their county administrator twice in the space of a week.
The second surprise came during Thursday’s commissioners meeting, when solicitor Robert Frycklund read a resolution honoring her for reaching a 45-year milestone in county service.
He smiled as he began reading Eloise Ahner’s many accomplishments in her four-decade tenure, which began in 1980 as a clerical aide trainee who was hired to the position in 1981.
Ahner moved on to clerk/steno a year later, and assistant chief clerk and loss control coordinator in 1988 and has served as county administrator/chief clerk since Feb. 2, 2012.
“Throughout her distinguished career, Eloise K. Ahner has been recognized for exceptional professionalism, dependability, extensive knowledge, leadership and commitment to the residents of Carbon County,” he said.
In 2021, the County Commissioners Association of Pennsylvania honored her as the Outstanding Chief Clerk/Administrator of the Year, recognizing her positive impact on the lives of county residents.
The award also highlighted her excellent work ethic, professionalism, interpersonal and leadership skills and extensive knowledge of issues affecting county residents.
“Her 45 years of service represents an extraordinary commitment to Carbon County and its residents, being a constant and trusted source of knowledge and continuity in Carbon County government,” Frycklund said.
“The Board of Commissioners of Carbon County,” he continued, “With heartfelt appreciation hereby honor and congratulation Eloise K. Ahner on 45 years of dedicated service to Carbon County and for her role in helping to make Carbon County a better place in which to live.”
Commissioner Chair Michael Sofranko said he can’t say enough about what Ahner does for the county, and how deeply she cares about residents, their concerns and every employee.
“She does an outstanding job for this county, she really does,” he said. “I personally don’t know where I’d be without her on a daily basis.”
Commissioner Wayne Nothstein, who has probably worked the longest with Ahner, said she has the most difficult job in the county for many reasons.
“The biggest reason is having to deal with the commissioners. Over the years, she had dealt with many, many commissioners,” he said. “She has had that quality that she would be able to smooth things over between commissioners through hell and high water, in rough times and bad times.
“I know that she has many sleepless nights and worries about the country as much as we do.”
“So, congratulations and thank you,” he told her.
Nothstein then shared the story of the first surprise, as one of the commissioners kept her occupied in her office as staffers set up a party with elected officials and county employees.
“Everybody in the building was scrambling. Trays were coming out of nowhere. We were hiding food and coolers in closets and on other floors,” Nothstein joked. “She was really overwhelmed in how we pulled it off.”
Ahner, who was presented with the resolution, thanked the commissioners, and all the commissioners who came before them, the wonderful office staff and all the department heads and elected officials.
“I’ll be here for a little bit yet,” she said with a lilt in her voice.
Commissioner Rocky Ahner said commissioners, especially him, give Ahner a hard time, but she does her job.
“That’s the main thing. She really does,” he said.

Title: Lansford ignores consultant's input – Times News Online
Article_Text:
Lansford ignores consultant’s input
Lansford Borough Council put its dysfunctional culture on full display a week after a consultant told members it needed to change to govern effectively.
Council members along with the public placed blame for a federal lawsuit that ended in a $230,000 settlement with a part-time police officer after council President Joe Genits asked if anyone had questions about it.
They sniped over using employee names in open discussions, complained about complaints and Right to Know law requests, and anyone defending another person then became the victim on another onslaught.
“No wonder we make the newspapers,” resident and former Councilwoman Rose Mary Cannon commented from the floor.
Councilman Joe Butrie agreed with her, saying simply, “Yes.”
One week earlier, consultant Ben Kafferlin told council a culture of hatred, distrust and bitterness was not conducive to progress and needed to change for the community for progress.
Kafferlin Strategies was hired to map out a five-year strategic plan and planning process under a state grant. Kafferlin suggested council’s culture needed to change before structural change could take place.
On Wednesday, following public comment, council moved onto its business, but the disagreement didn’t end there.
Council was set to move on enrolling its borough secretary Ashley McLaughlin and code officer Shane Monk in the Pennsylvania Municipal Retirement System in accordance with their work agreements, but tabled action.
Councilman Bruce Markovich questioned which plan they were choosing, and Councilwoman Michele Bartek said she contacted the actuaries, Foster and Foster, for more information.
They agreed to discuss the matter further in their October workshop meeting, when Markovich mentioned the pension plan the water authority has for its employees being one of the best.
Resident Tommy Vadyak, who sits on the water authority board, agreed, and said that Markovich, a former council president, had all the information.
That prompted questions from Genits regarding the time frame for granting McLaughlin a pension, which was promised when she was hired more than two years ago.
“OK, but my question is, you say you had it over there, why is it taking so long if you have it?” Genits asked Markovich.
“I don’t come into this office, Joe. I have no reason,” Markovich responded, as Genits asked why not.
“Because I can’t stand you,” Markovich asserted, “It’s as simple as that. I cannot stand you. I can’t stand to be in the office with you if you want the truth.”
Genits then thanked Markovich for an email earlier that day and asked if he wanted him to pass out copies.
“I don’t care what you do with it,” Markovich said.
Genits did not disclose what the email was about. He then asked Markovich how many times he complimented the work that he had done in the past and asked for his help.
“You don’t like it because George (Gilbert) was elected president and I moved up the ladder,” Genits said, referring to the former council president who resigned in January after two weeks in the post, leaving him to take over as vice president.
“And look at the mess we’re in right now,” Markovich said.
Genits asked what mess and then blamed Markovich for the same.
“Because you caused it,” Genits said. “Including the Diaz lawsuit.”
Genits earlier blamed Markovich for not reviewing or signing an insurance renewal, which was completed by the former treasurer, Maria Ahner, for the lack of insurance for the lawsuit.
During that same volley, Mayor Denise Leibensperger also blamed Markovich, who was council president at the time, for not reporting a claim to the insurance company, leaving the borough on the hook for the settlement.
Then residents Vadyak and Erin Soberick blamed council for not taking proper action regarding Diaz and preventing the lawsuit and need for coverage.
Following the Genits-Markovich blowup, council slid into finishing the pension discussion, noting that there was money owed retroactively, and Bartek saying she had the code officer’s information.
That topic exhausted, Butrie then quietly asked council to “Continue, please.”
Council was just concluding the second item on its agenda and the meeting, which began at 7 p.m., was already nearly an hour in duration.
Council began earlier in the day with an executive session for personnel for Monk, the code officer, to discuss a “hostile” work environment and the interviewing of secretarial candidates following the resignation of its treasurer.
Council had planned on hiring someone at the special meeting but decided to withdraw a motion to offer one of the five candidates the full-time position to give members time to discuss and consider them all.
Immediately before, council agreed to grant its borough secretary McLaughlin unpaid leave from Oct. 9 to Oct. 18.
She will not attend the next council meeting Oct. 14. McLaughlin will return Oct. 19 to process payroll. Council did not discuss whether the borough office would be open during her absence.

Title: Tamaqua Area facilities to be assessed – Times News Online
Article_Text:
Tamaqua Area facilities to be assessed
Tamaqua Area School Board moved ahead with a one-year contract with a national facility and planning construction firm.
The board approved the no-cost contract with SitelogIQ to perform a districtwide facility assessment that will give the district a road map for capital project planning and maintenance.
The contract is at no cost to the district with the caveat that the district allow Tamaqua Area’s aggregated data in a statewide facility study to be presented to lawmakers.
The firm is lobbying Pennsylvania to resurrect the state’s PlanCon Program, which reimbursed districts for major building renovations and construction.
Sound system
The board also approved the purchase and installation of a new sound system for the Tamaqua Elementary School.
The district chose Event Staging Inc. of Orwigsburg, which is a COSTAR vendor, for the project, which should not exceed $25,000.
The sound system is original to the building, and the stage is being used for more robust activities, such as productions and plays, Kenneth Dunkelberger, chief operations officer, said.
This would be for a full-fledged sound system with all new wiring and mounted on the ceiling, he said.
Other
The board in other business approved these items:
• An agreement with Penn State Hazleton Campus for the use of the high school baseball field at a negotiated price, contingent upon submission of necessary documentation.
• An agreement with Helping Harvest Fresh Food Bank, Reading, as a host site for product distribution.
• The second reading of Policy No. 918, Title I Parent and Family Engagement.
• Homebound instruction for one elementary student.
• An affiliation agreement with Moravian University for student practicum experience.
• The resolution identifying and authorizing the superintendent to sign electronic agreements with the state Department of Education.
• The business administrator to approve repository sales and process payments and other routine items.
• A resolution to vote for a list of candidates for the Pennsylvania School Board Association board of directors.

Title: LVHN Health Care Partner of the Month – Times News Online
