Title: Where We Live: Time spent with Dad magic – Times News Online
Article_Text:
Where We Live: Time spent with Dad magic
Although my dad passed away 22 years ago, I carry his spirit with me every day. I always felt that I had a special closeness with him as I admired his integrity, humor and kindness.
There were many times in my childhood where my dad and I did things — just the two of us, not including my mom or my older or younger sister.
One of the most memorable was going to see the musical, “The Magic Show.” Although I was around 13 years old, I still remember the song “I Want to Be a Lion Tamer.” The lyrics strike me funny now but it was a great memory.
My dad had a love of magic, and he and I would go to magic shops and find the coolest, newest trick. That’s where I learned the keys to magic: “Never reveal your secret” and “never do the same trick twice in front of the same audience.”
We went to a magic show at the former Painted Bride in Philadelphia. It was three comedic magicians called The Asparagus Valley Cultural Society. Two of those performers were Penn and Teller. I love to say that I saw them way back when. I always wonder what happened to the third person.
I couldn’t have been more than 12, but I remember somebody played the xylophone and one of the magic tricks consisted of someone dressed as a gorilla appearing on the balcony, which made everyone look up as on stage suddenly things “disappeared” while the audience’s eyes were averted.
What these memories are really about is the time shared with my dad and feeling so connected and special.
My friend’s son celebrates his birthday by doing one-on-one activities with each of his three boys. What a wonderful way to celebrate each other.
Another memory I have is when my dad took me to use my new skateboard. It was unforgettable because, unfortunately, while using my skateboard, my dad fell and broke his leg. I was too young to drive at the time and I know the pain he was in as he drove himself to the hospital.
Breaking my own ankle as an adult, I realized how my dad never complained as he went to work in the city (Philly) with crutches by bus and El every single day. We did have a “cast off” party for him, as my mom was always ready to entertain and she was a magnificent party thrower.
My parents always encouraged my interests, from buying me a “dummy” (which I still have) to be a ventriloquist, and a unicycle, which I did teach myself to ride with a stick my dad “made” to help me get on it.
There were times when my dad and I argued. I have two letters he wrote to me after arguing. One is from the year I graduated from high school, and the other from the year I graduated from grad school.
What still astounds me is that his messages to me were loving and forgiving, encouraging me to trust myself. I realized he was in his early 40s when he wrote the first letter, and it amazes me even more how he so readily acknowledged what happened and found a path to resolution.
The time spent with your children is precious and meaningful. It doesn’t have to involve spending; it could literally be a walk in the park. Finding common ground or sharing something new makes it unforgettable.
Whether a “girl dad,” “boy dad,” “girl mom” or “boy mom,” the memories shared have an infinite value.

Title: 'Where do you go?' — Archbald residents fear giant data center next door
Article_Text:
ARCHBALD — Meg and Kim Nudelman spend most mornings sipping coffee on their patio in a quiet backyard on Foxtail Circle, sitting in green wicker chairs and looking out onto rows of pine and birch trees.
The Nudelman sisters used to enjoy seeing the wildlife — birds, foxes, black bears and even the occasional snapping turtle — from the solace of their enclosed patio decorated with vibrant floral carpets and potted plants, but now, the two spend their time trying to figure out ways to stop Lackawanna County’s single largest data center from moving into their backyard.
Lurking just behind the thin treeline separating the Nudelmans’ townhouse from the former Highway Auto Parts junkyard, work is underway to prepare 70-plus acres for Project Boson — a 619,925-square-foot data center proposed by a company affiliated with Kriger Construction Inc., 99 Power Blvd., Archbald.
With a footprint larger than 10½ football fields, Project Boson borders the Highlands Archbald housing development off Eynon Jermyn Road on two sides. Just across the street, the same developer is seeking approval from Archbald for a 400-megawatt Essential Energy LLC natural gas power plant near Archbald’s Staback Park.
“I feel it’s going to be the death of me,” said Meg Nudelman, 66, a two-time breast cancer survivor with bad asthma. “But where do you go? We’re not young.”
Meg and her sister, Kim Nudelman, 75, moved into their townhouse nine years ago to settle into in their older years, enjoying the peace of a largely retirement-age street. That changed last year when Archbald Data & Energy Center LLC filed land development plans and a zoning permit application for Project Boson, initially proposing three data centers before merging them into one giant building. Other companies tied to Kriger Construction propose four data centers and three natural gas power plants across Bell Mountain in Dickson City.
“It never even entered our mind,” Meg Nudelman said, discussing the prospect of a massive data center and power plant near their home. “It’s so peaceful. … We got it because it was one-floor living for our older years that we could navigate.”
While Project Boson does not need conditional-use approval from Archbald council, it still requires final land development approval from the borough, as well as permitting from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection.
In its review of Project Boson’s National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit application, otherwise known as its stormwater permit, the DEP identified technical deficiencies across 23 categories. The Aug. 26 letter provided about 140 comments ranging from minimizing stormwater to existing soil contamination and lack of investigation into potential groundwater contamination from a junkyard that had operated for nearly 70 years.
There are 51 data centers proposed in Archbald across six projects, with another developer considering at least two more data centers in the Valley View Business Park.
‘Reduce stormwater volume’
PDC Realty LLC, 99 Power Blvd., Archbald, purchased the former junkyard in August 2025 for $1.575 million. Kriger Construction President Jim Marzolino most recently signed a corrective deed for the property in August as a member of PDC, according to Lackawanna County recorder of deeds filings.
Kriger Construction is listed as the equitable owner of the property in its Aug. 18, 2025, major land development preliminary plan filed in Archbald; Kriger Construction Vice President David Stiles signed Project Boson’s subdivision/land development application the same day.
Marzolino declined to comment when reached by phone Friday. Emailed requests for comment from Stiles were unsuccessful.
Although data centers are no longer allowed in the general commercial land bordering the Highlands, the developer applied in Archbald before the borough restricted its zoning in November to regulate data centers. By applying before Archbald amended its zoning, the development is grandfathered under a principal permitted use designation that forgoes the conditional-use hearings used to regulate other projects like Wildcat Ridge and Project Green Mountain.
Project Boson’s zoning permit application describes just over 1.6 million square feet of impervious area, meaning buildings, parking lots, roads and other structures that water can’t permeate, covering about 43% of the 3.75-million-square-foot site.
In its technical deficiency letter, which is part of a back-and-forth exchange where the DEP identifies issues and gives the applicant a window to address them in a response, the department notes that Project Boson would increase stormwater runoff by 210,439 cubic feet in the event of a two-year storm, which is a storm that has a 50% chance of happening in any given year. That means during a bad storm, Project Boson could generate nearly 1.6 million gallons of runoff.
“The Department recommends the applicant explore other options to reduce stormwater volume,” the DEP reports, recommending that, “Due to increase in volume coming from the site, easements from the downslope property owners are suggested.”
‘Too close to residences’
Bernie McGurl has spent the past 40 years working with Northeast Pennsylvania’s waterways, including 32 years as the executive director of the Lackawanna River Conservation Association. Although he stepped down from executive director, he remains a senior project manager for the group.
After reviewing the deficiency letter and its recommendation to seek out easements from nearby properties, McGurl came to a simple conclusion: “There’s no place to put the stormwater up there.”
“What the mining companies did 150 years ago was disrupt, disturb, destroy all of the drainage areas. The topography of the landscape was turned inside out to mine the coal, both underground and then surface strip mining activities, and that ruptured the flow of water across the surface of the valley,” McGurl said. “Some of the water will infiltrate down through the broken rock and soils into the subterranean mine pool into the huge complex of mine voids under the valley, but that’s not something that we really want to encourage because it has to be treated. It comes out into the (Lackawanna) river as mine drainage.”
While some abandoned mine lands could support data centers, McGurl stressed his opposition to the developments, especially Project Boson’s location.
“I don’t think there’s a spot in the valley right now that’s appropriate. One or two of them could have some potential, but the sites in Archbald are definitely not appropriate,” McGurl said. “They’re too close to residences. They need to be at least a mile away — preferably more.”
Generating nearly 1.6 million gallons of runoff during a bad rainstorm is significant near neighborhoods, he said.
“It’s going to fill up the street in front of your house with 3-4 inches of flowing water really quickly, and maybe up to a foot and cause a lot of flash flooding around the facility,” he said. “I don’t think we ever anticipated any kind of development at this scale in the valley.”
‘That soil is toast’
Beyond stormwater issues, the DEP’s deficiency letter addressed the site’s contamination from the longtime junkyard.
The review notes that a January 2025 environmental site assessment found benzene and other chemicals in concentrations exceeding residential concentrations near a former 275-gallon storage tank, but a remediation report submitted July 31 did not include that area of concern. Neither the site assessment nor report included a groundwater investigation, so it’s unknown if groundwater contamination is present, according to DEP.
“Due to the scale and historical usage of the site, remaining soil contamination may be present in areas not characterized or remediated in previous environmental investigations,” the DEP wrote, recommending that workers wear personal protective equipment during remediation and construction.
Asked about whether he expects groundwater contamination, McGurl chuckled for about 10 seconds before saying, “I hope your recording machine is picking up the laughter — yeah, that soil is toast.”
“It’s a brownfield site, so you have to treat it like there’s hazardous materials in the soil, and the hazardous materials in the soil when they get wet, they get taken up by the water — stormwater or infiltration into groundwater — and when they’re dry, and they get kicked around, they become airborne,” he continued.
‘Needs to be addressed immediately’
Tamara Misewicz-Healey, an industrial hygienist and mother of three young children in Archbald, has spent the past year fighting data centers after co-founding the Stop Archbald Data Centers movement with her husband, Justin Healey.
Project Boson raises serious concerns next to the Highlands and across the street from the borough’s Staback Park, she said.
“When you’re looking at contaminants like that, those are carcinogens, neurotoxins, and with those, there’s really not a safe limit,” Misewicz-Healey said. “It’s just the more you’re exposed, the higher your risk gets.”
If soil isn’t properly removed from the site, strong winds can blow the dust into nearby communities, she said. Even if residents don’t inhale it, the dust could coat playgrounds and yards, exposing residents through their skin. Runoff from the rain can also carry it into streams and rivers, she said.
“There are a lot of questions that should be explored, and I think this needs to be addressed immediately,” she said.
Numerous studies have linked benzene exposure to blood cancers — lymphomas, she said.
“Children are especially susceptible to environmental carcinogens as their bodies are developing at a higher rate — higher rates of replication — and they don’t have the full mechanisms that we do as adults,” Misewicz-Healey said. “They also have different behavioral practices, so their heart rate is quicker, so they tend to breathe a lot more air per their body mass, so they have that higher route of exposure through inhalation. But they also generally have higher rates of exposure through dermal because they touch everything.”
She contends Archbald’s previous zoning, even when it principally permitted data centers in commercial zones without defining them, was intended for small-scale commercial data centers — not an industrial hyperscale building like Project Boson.
“It should just absolutely not be in the location it’s being proposed in,” she said. “It should be in a heavy industrial zone, well away from community everyday life.”
Misewicz-Healey also worried about the impacts on the numerous older residents living in the Highlands.
‘This can’t happen’
Living next to a junkyard wasn’t much of a disturbance for the Nudelman sisters. Sometimes they would see an old school bus through the treeline when the leaves fall in the autumn or they’d hear a worker pulling parts from a vehicle, but it didn’t really bother them.
Project Boson changed that.
Getting up from her kitchen table, Meg Nudelman picked up a black pouch with a decibel meter in it that she keeps next to the kitchen window facing Project Boson, explaining she and her sister monitor the noise next door. As Meg Nudelman demonstrated the meter, her sister flipped through a calendar, with decibel readings scribbled under each date.
“When they were cutting down the trees, it got to 57 (decibels),” Kim Nudelman said.
Archbald’s zoning ordinance limits maximum daytime decibel levels to 55 dBA at residential property lines.
Noise and air emissions have emerged as two central concerns surrounding the bus-sized backup generators that data centers rely on during power outages.
When Archbald adopted its standards for data centers in November, it exempted backup generators from noise restrictions during testing and outages, but that waiver won’t apply to Project Boson under the legacy zoning allowing it to proceed as a principal permitted use.
Fleets of diesel generators put out significantly more fine particulate matter — tiny particles 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair — than natural gas power plants with the same output. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency cites numerous studies linking exposure to health problems, including premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function and increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing or difficulty breathing.
That’s especially concerning for a cancer survivor with asthma like Meg Nudelman.
As the Nudelmans shared their concerns about the cumulative effects of data centers, their doorbell rang. Their neighbors, Karen and Jim Timmons, stopped by to visit. The Timmonses have lived on Foxtail Circle for a decade.
A cancer survivor herself, Karen Timmons, 70, has testified at public hearings in Archbald to emphasize the impacts of data centers and a power plant on herself and her neighbors.
Kim and Meg Nudelman initially taught them about data centers, and as the Timmonses learned more about the developments, they became increasingly horrified.
“Oh my God, this can’t happen,” Karen Timmons said. “We can’t have this in Kim and Meg’s backyard, let alone across from us.”
Nearly all of their neighbors are 65 or older, she said.
“The air emissions are especially of concern for vulnerable groups,” she said. “All four of us do feel an obligation to take care of the neighborhood.”
As a retired educator, Jim Timmons, 73, spent 11 years as an assistant principal and later principal in the Valley View School District, whose nearest school is less than half a mile from Project Boson on Columbus Drive.
“I don’t understand how any of this could be so close to this neighborhood, all the homes back here and the school district,” he said.
He described a sense of helplessness.
“The morality of all this is squashed,” Jim Timmons said. “There’s no morality with this.”
The DEP gave Project Boson until Sept. 25 to respond to its deficiency letter, or else the department could deny or withdraw the application. Alternatively, if the developer does not believe the deficiencies can be fully addressed within the time frame, it should consider a voluntary withdrawal, according to DEP.
If the project moves forward, McGurl wants the DEP to “hold their feet to the fire.”
“When it starts to rain and you get a heavy storm, you’re going to find out, and I don’t think we need to do that,” McGurl said. “Let them figure out a way to say, ‘Hey, we’re going to be the most responsible, absurd stormwater managers on the planet.’”

Title: Donald Trump's wild week as he bans media from White House and brags over Greenland 'deal'
Article_Text:
Donald Trump's wild week as he bans media from White House and brags over Greenland 'deal'
Donald Trump is an old man backed into a corner, and he's grasping for anything he can control
Donald Trump has suffered a series of humiliations over the last few weeks. From the Supreme Court ruling his plan to screw up the midterms by making postal voting insanely complicated couldn't be implemented in time, to his hand-picked Fed chair voting through a rate increase...to another judge saying he can't write his name on the memorial to a dead president, it's been defeat after defeat.
And despite offering the American people a $5,000 bribe each and urging them to pretend he's on the ballot, it looks increasingly like his Republican Party is going to lose both houses of Congress in November's election.
And when you're an old man backed into a corner, being told left and right that you can't do the things you want to do, you grab onto pretty much anything you can control.
And that's probably why Trump announced last night that three news outlets would be banned from the White House and made out a fairly benign treaty extension with Denmark was a major shift in power over Greenland.
Here's how Trump's week spiralled, and how he's now trying to claw his way back.
"Oh, the ban on the free press?"
Donald Trump last night announced he was throwing CNN, Politico and MS Now out of the White House, something he genuinely referred to as a "ban on the free press."
Why? Well, because he doesn't like the things they write.
Claiming the outlets were "unfair" and "dishonest", Trump said it was a "very simple ban. I don't want them in my office, I don't want them here. I would say the ban will go as far as you can. If they could straighten themselves out I'd love it."
He went on to warn the New York Times and Washington Post they could be next.
Trump tried to ban now former CNN reporter Jim Acosta from the White House during his first term, taking his White House pass away from him.
But the move was blocked by a federal court after Acosta argued it infringed on his rights under the first amendment (freedom of the press) and fifth amendment (due process).
Asked if he was trying to "intimidate" the press, Trump said: "No, no, no. I dislike dishonest press, like you, I think you're terrible. I like to see honest press."
Asked how the move was constitutional, Trump said: "I don't think someone should be allowed to come in and write fake stories....It's sick. There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories. Now, if they want to write them that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my...into the people's house."
At the time of writing, reporters are starting to arrive at the White House to find their passes have been deactivated.
As it stands, CNN is still down to be the nominated pool outlet travelling with Trump on Monday, so we'll see.
"We've got Greenland!"
Trump last night posted a message on Truth Social that seemed to suggest Denmark had kind of given Greenland to the US. He followed that up by posting a map of the country overlaid with the Stars and Stripes.
And it's certainly been taken that way by a decent chunk of MAGA - with Utah Senator Mike Lee tweeting: "We've got Greenland! This is what winning looks like."
But it ain't really so, though, Joe.
Trump said on Friday that the agreement would give the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.”Denmark and the US already have a long-standing security agreement that has allowed the US to deploy forces in Greenland, and it was not immediately clear how this deal was different from that.
The deal is expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York, which Trump will attend from Monday.
"Sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift"
So you might remember earlier this year that Donald Trump's adult son, Don Jr, got married for the second time. It made a bit of news at the time, because the ceremony took place in the Bahamas and Trump...the father of the groom...did not go.
His excuse was that he was a little busy with the Iran war. And, sure, maybe.
But we learned this week that while the wedding itself was a smallish affair in a chapel on a private island, there was a two-day after party on a different island, which was paid for by Umar Kremlev a Russian Oligarch with close ties to Vladimir Putin.
The island rents for about a hundred thousand dollars a night, and other costs covered by Kremlev are said to have included a fireworks display that cost another 70 grand.
Jr's new wife Bettina, described Kremlev as a "dear friend" and said he "very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us after our wedding."
She went on to say: "It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful"
Jr's people said he and Kremlev are "personal friends" but don't have a business relationship.
And the happy couple added: "It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from.
"Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift."
So who is this guy? Well, Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association, which is funded by the Russian state-backed energy firm Gazprom.
The group has been suspended by the Olympics, in part, for failing to report its ties to Gazprom.
As recently as this year, Kremlev was part of a Russian delegation to China led by Putin himself. Putin has also given Kremlev the Order of Friendship, one of the Russian Federation's highest honours.
Donald Trump senior said: "I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn't pay for Don and Bettina's wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day."
And last night in the Oval Office Trump said he had "heard" that Don Jr had reimbursed Kremlev for the cost of the festivities - which, assuming it's true (and we shouldn't assume that...) raises the question of...why? If it's all totally above board and fine, why pay it back?
Also, the Trump family is, famously, a billionaire family. Jr's personal net worth is in the region of $300 million.
Why didn't he just pay for his own party? I suspect we'll find out one day. Maybe some time before the LA Olympics.
"I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Center"
Long term readers will recall that Donald Trump has an obsession with the Kennedy Centre.
For newcomers, a quick recap: The Kennedy Centre is - or was - America's most renowned performing arts venue and organisation. A bit like The Barbican, except it's also the official national monument for John F Kennedy - one of America's most beloved presidents. A President, we should note, whose disappointing adult nephew serves in Trump's cabinet. More of him in a moment.
Trump set his sights on it from day one of his second Presidency, mounting a coup to stuff the board with his own cronies and installing himself as chairman. He set about reforming it in his own image, changing the programme in a way that prompted a huge backlash plunging ticket sales. He also, in the dead of night, added his own name above the door - so it was officially called the Donald J Trump and the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Literally people woke up to find he'd slapped his name on a presidential memorial. Why is he so obsessed with taking over this hallowed institution? Well, nobody really knows. But throughout history dictators have seized control of the creative arts to suppress dissent and break up alternatives to state propaganda. To be clear, I'm not saying Trump is a dictator. But I am saying he's read a few pages from the big book of things that dictators do.
Anyway, the courts, unsurprisingly told him, nah, can't do that. See congress if you want to change the name. So the name had to come down. Fast forward to a month or so ago and Trump's handpicked board came up with another plan. According to them, the building is in drastic need of repair. Now, we only have their word and some CCTV footage of bits falling off the ceiling for that. And this is the trump administration, so we definitely shouldn't take that at face value. Remember the thing with the reflecting pool?
They said Trump was willing to close the centre for repairs, and he'd ensure the funding was there to renovate - IF the courts agree to put his name back up on the wall. In smaller letters this time, and underneath JFK's name rather than on top. And a federal judge blocked both the closure and the name change.
On Tuesday, the board closed the building anyway, in defiance of the judge's ruling. The same day, there was a reportedly chaotic meeting of the centre's board, during which they voted for a third time to close the building. This was opposed by Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat ex officio board member, who is behind the lawsuit that is blocking the process in the courts.
After that, Trump issued a pretty ominous statement on Truth Social. If the courts ruled against his appeal, and refused to let him put his name on the wall, he said, "the reconstruction and the renovation of the Kennedy Center will not take place." The centre would close "immediately" - and there was no indication of when...or if.. it would reopen.
And then came the photos. Trump landed at Andrews Air Force Base after a speech in North Carolina, and a photographer snapped him looking at a big poster board, on which is clearly written "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED". The picture isn't clear, but it appears to be a manipulated image of the centre.
Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the centre, which he claimed was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it.
“We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it," he said. "I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Center.”
Later last night, supporters and patrons descended on the legendary building, forming a human chain around it in protest against Trump's apparent plans.
Remember what happened with the East Wing. Do not be surprised if you wake up one morning in the near future to see footage of bulldozers.
"You've got a friend in the White House"
Robert F Kennedy Jr told members of an anti-vaccine group he founded that they have a "steadfast friend at the White House".
RFK, who is Donald Trump's health secretary, was speaking at a convention of Children's Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade.
His speech came after four people did of measles in Pennsylvania, in the worst outbreak of the disease in decades.
"Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago," he said.
Kennedy, who is not a medical professional, raised a string of baseless questions about long-established vaccine safety.
He boasted about how the Trump administration, under his guidance, had limited the number of life-saving vaccines routinely given to children in the US - including scrapping regular shots for hepatitis A and B and meningococcal, the rare virus that causes meningitis.
President Trump has made repeated and unfounded claims that the vaccine scheme was "dangerous" and contributed to increased autism diagnoses.
And Trump suggested falsely that the Measles, Mumps and Rubella (MMR) vaccine could be "quite lethal" if taken as combined injection, and called for it to be split in to three separate shots.
Some 3,294 cases of measles have been confirmed in the US so far in 2026, up from 2,289 in the whole of 2025. according to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). Nearly half of the 2026 cases (45%) were in children and young people aged 5-19, with 18% of the cases affecting the under 5s.
Some 95% of the cases were in unvaccinated people, or people whose vaccination status was unknown. Just 3% had had both doses of MMR. Of the 2026 cases, 267 people were hospitalised, including 66 children under 5.
In 2024, the year before Trump returned to office, there were 285 cases, and in 2023 just 59. More cases of measles have been confirmed in the US so far this year than in the decade from 2014 to 2024.
RFK spoke alongside Andrew Wakefield, the disgraced British former doctor whose fabricated research first popularised the false claim that the MMR vaccine is linked to autism.
After being struck off in the UK, and ostracised by the medical community, Wakefield moved to the US, where he has since become a minor celebrity in the anti-vaccine world.

Title: Skill game operators face Oct. 13 deadline to remove machines
Article_Text:
Skill game operators face Oct. 13 deadline to remove machines
Pennsylvania residents may have less than a month remaining to play their favorite skill games, the casino-like machines that currently dot small businesses across the state.
Unless Pennsylvania lawmakers carve out a legislative fix to allow skill games to continue to operate, local businesses will be forced to remove or deactivate their machines by Oct. 13, according to a June ruling from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. The court ruled skill games are legally no different from slot machines.
The ruling ensured skill games would be fall under the laws that govern slot machines, which can only be placed in casinos.
In recent years, a number of establishments have popped up throughout Pennsylvania solely dedicated to offering spaces with multiple skill game machines for play. One of these is Poo’s Place in Summit Township, operated by 71-year-old Ed Skillman, who has 14 machines.
Skillman said, without prompt action from the state, he may have to shut his business down.
“We are literally just in limbo,” Skillman said. “I don’t want to talk politics right now, but as bad as our economy is right now and all the taxes we have and the rising costs of everything, I don’t think the legislators have thought this through with how many people they’re going to put on unemployment and companies out of business by making these things illegal. That’s just my opinion.”
According to state Sen. Elder Vogel, R-47th, Democrats and Republicans in the General Assembly are still far apart on how they propose to regulate skill games.
“While Senate Republicans were open to … using revenues from skill games for transit so long as there was accountability, Democrats have been reluctant to come to the table, as they want free reign to use the money for spending with no guardrails,” Vogel said.
One of the key debate topics in negotiations for the 2026-27 Pennsylvania state budget was the question of how — or whether — to tax skill games to provide additional revenue. In his initial pitch for the budget, Gov. Josh Shapiro suggested a 52% tax. Ultimately, the final version of the state budget, which was signed in July, left skill game legislation and taxation unaddressed.
Two pieces of legislation were proposed in Pennsylvania to regulate skill games: Senate Bill 1079, sponsored by Sen. Gene Yaw, R-23rd, and House Bill 2213, sponsored by Rep. Danilo Burgos, D-197th. Both bills aim to establish a $500 monthly fee for skill game terminals and limit the total number of skill games in Pennsylvania to 50,000. No vote has taken place on either bill.
Pace-O-Matic, one of the main providers of skill game machines in Pennsylvania, has warned of dire consequences for Pennsylvania’s economy and small businesses if no decision is reached by mid-October.
“Small businesses, including restaurants and taverns across the state, say they will close their doors, lay off staff and stop donating to community causes if commonsense skill game legislation doesn’t pass by the Oct. 13 deadline,” wrote a spokesperson for Pace-O-Matic. “Along with small businesses, American Legion and VFW posts, volunteer fire companies and fraternal clubs — such as Elk and Moose lodges, will be devastated by losing the revenue from Pennsylvania Skill games. Many veteran organizations, in particular, have repeatedly said during the last few months that they will be forced to close without skill games.”
One club that could be impacted is American Legion Post 117 on Butler’s Main Street, which features several skill game machines in its club room. Post adjutant Dean Noechel said that a loss of revenue from skill games could adversely impact the post’s operations.
“It’s going to impact the donations that we give to our local community,” Noechel said. “It’s going to affect the donations that we give to the high school kids. We use that money to pay our utility bills and stuff like that as well. That money is used to keep our organization open and able to support our mission of helping veterans.”
Noechel says he’s spoken to state Rep. Marcie Mustello, R-11th, as well as someone from the office of state Sen. Scott Hutchinson, R-21st, about the issue.
“They said that they’re aware and they're trying to work on legislation to help,” Noechel said.
On the other hand, Chris Silverio, president of the Chicora Moose Lodge, has taken a neutral stance on the issue. Although the lodge on West Slippery Rock Street has a few skill game machines, Silverio said the revenue from them is not vital and his club will survive without it if he has to unplug the machines.
“The Chicora Moose has functioned for years without those skill games,” Silverio said. “It’s nice to have, but it's not necessary to keep our business open.”
Assuming skill games end up barred, a state police spokesman told the Butler Eagle the agency’s plan of enforcement would lean on voluntary deactivation.
“In the absence of legislative action, the Pennsylvania State Police will be prepared to enforce the law consistent with the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s decision,” deputy communications director Chris Caracino said. “PSP is currently developing an enforcement plan for implementation beginning Oct. 14. That plan will strongly encourage voluntary compliance and provide businesses and operators an opportunity to voluntarily remove unlawful machines.”
“We want to be clear that we will follow the law and if there is no skill game legislation by Oct. 13, Pennsylvania Skill will shut down all its games across the commonwealth,” Pace-O-Matic said.

Title: Peter McManus: The last of the 'Molly Maguires' | Local News
Article_Text:
SUNBURY — On Oct. 9, 1879, an Irish coal miner named Peter McManus was hanged in the courtyard of the Northumberland County Prison, a year after being found guilty of murder. He was the last alleged member of the Molly Maguires — a secretive group of Irish coal miners who fought against poor labor conditions with violence — to ever be executed.
Across Pennsylvania’s coal region, Irish coal miners allegedly organized as the Molly Maguires in the mid-19th century in response to horrific working conditions and long hours spent underground for poor wages. Mine disasters, an economic depression in 1873 and crackdowns on labor unions further contributed to their grievances with their employers — and led some to engage in vigilante violence.

Title: Atlanta Braves clinch 8th playoff berth in 9 years with victory over Astros
Article_Text:
Atlanta Braves clinch 8th playoff berth in 9 years with victory over Astros
HOUSTON (AP) — The Atlanta Braves held a subdued celebration when they clinched a playoff berth Friday night after missing out last season.
The first-place Braves beat the Houston Astros 6-2 to punch their ticket to the postseason for the eighth time in nine years. They secured at least a National League wild card and reduced their magic number to three for winning the NL East.
Afterward there was no wild celebration, but rather a simple toast with bubbly before they began looking ahead.
“We've got our eyes on bigger and better things,” outfielder Michael Harris II said. “We’re trying to win the East. So got to go out there and do what we know we can do and hopefully we can celebrate big for that.”
First-year manager Walt Weiss echoed the sentiment shared by Harris.
“Everything you get in this league is earned,” Weiss said. “I’ve said it a few times this year, but great group, what they’ve overcome this year, and hopefully some bigger celebrations ahead.”
Harris, Ronald Acuña Jr. and Matt Olson each hit a two-run homer to help the Braves bounce back after dropping two of three games to the Chicago Cubs this week.
Advertisement
Atlanta is trying to hold off the Philadelphia Phillies for the NL East title and could wrap up the division crown as soon as Sunday. Atlanta’s win Friday night coupled with Philadelphia’s 6-3 loss to the Mets gave the Braves a five-game lead over the Phillies with eight to play.
Weiss was asked about helping the team back to the playoffs in his first season as manager after spending eight seasons as Brian Snitker’s bench coach.
“I always say it’s always about the players,” Weiss said. “They’re the ones out there performing. We've got a good staff. When you accomplish things, it’s an organizational effort. ... It takes everybody and we've got a really good group.”
If the Braves take the division, it will be their seventh NL East championship in nine years.
Atlanta's return to the playoffs comes after a disappointing 2025 season in which the team went 76-86 and finished fourth in the division, snapping a streak of seven straight playoff appearances that included six consecutive NL East titles from 2018-23. That run was highlighted by beating the Astros to win the 2021 World Series.
Friday’s victory gave the Braves 90 wins, marking the fifth time in the last eight full seasons that they’ve reached the mark. The only teams with more 90-win seasons in that stretch are the Dodgers with eight and the Brewers and Yankees with six apiece.

Title: This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
Article_Text:
This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
YARDLEY, Pa. (AP) — Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing.
But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party's congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.
Until now.
This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.
Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that “I don't see it happening.”
Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick’s reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump’s recent midterm convention in Dallas.
But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president’s sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.
Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year's political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote.
“That’s the job,” he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview.
Democrats have tried for years to defeat Fitzpatrick
Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms.
“The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for,” he said in an interview this summer. “I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation.”
Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points.
“Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway,” said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. “It’s, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time.”
Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick.
“I’m not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that’s very, very different than any race he’s ever run before,” he said.

Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump's immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party's leaders.
“He's a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community,” she said. But, she added, “you have to serve everyone in your district."
Fitzpatrick has been willing to criticize Trump
Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020.
Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.
“You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart,” Rachau said.
In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV “weak,” and captive to the “Radical Left."
“There’s so many angry voices out there. We all know that's the case,” Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. “People are sick and tired of the noise. They’re sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about.”
Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church's parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.
Fitzpatrick spends millions on attack ads against Harvie
Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.
According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged.
The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.
No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker’s lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other.
Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president.
“Incumbents just feel they can’t cross that line. If they do, they’re not going to get reelected," she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. "They might not get reelected anyway.”

Title: Ed Sheeran is set to return to stage for 1st time since Macklemore was cut and other acts withdrew
Article_Text:
By TASSANEE VEJPONGSA
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Ed Sheeran is set to resume his tour Saturday — possibly solo — after all his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.
It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original U.S. opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.
Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.
Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists’ support. As of Saturday afternoon, tickets were still available for the show, and his website did not list any replacement acts.
A group of about 50 pro-Palestinian demonstrators rallied outside the stadium. Rose Tejada, 20, of Philadelphia, expressed disappointment that Sheeran did not take a stand on the issue.
“This is endemic in Western culture that we believe we can stay out of conflict, be apolitical,” Tejada said.
The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey. Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday.
Within hours of Sheeran’s statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.
Jessica Grono, 51, planned to drive 30 minutes from her Phoenixville home to attend the concert. She has liked Sheeran since his song “The A Team” was released in 2011 and loves his voice, music and storytelling.
“I feel bad for him,” Grono said, adding that he has not said anything wrong and should not be penalized for others’ words.
Macklemore said Wednesday he is donating $1 million to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift; a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million but have not specified where the money will be directed. Sheeran’s representatives have not responded to multiple requests for comment.
Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the No. 3 top-earning concert act since 2021.
Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.
The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn’t be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.
He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.
While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran’s magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

The 5 Illnesses Doctors Say Are ‘Already On The Rise’ This Fall — And How To Tell Them Apart
After months of outdoor summer fun, kids are back in school — shared germs and all.
These germs spread quickly and easily beyond school to parents, aunts, uncles, grandparents and babysitters, who then spread those germs on to colleagues, friends and passersby, leading to lots of sniffling and coughing throughout the United States.

“Respiratory viruses are already on the rise,” said Dr. Alexa Mieses Malchuk, a family physician in Pennsylvania. And there are specific illnesses that are showing up more and more in patients this fall.
Doctors share the viruses they’re seeing during this back-to-school season:
1. Common colds caused by viruses like rhinovirus and parainfluenza
“It is very typical for us to see respiratory tract infections when school gets back into session,” said Dr. Richard Martinello, the chief medical officer of Yale Medicine and an infectious diseases specialist. Respiratory tract infections often cause the symptoms folks associate with a cold, such as cough, runny nose, congestion, sore throat, sneezing and fever.
“We’ve been seeing a lot of respiratory-type things — a lot of runny noses, congestion, cough ... the common cold type stuff,” said Dr. Moses F. Olorunnisola, a pediatrician at Hackensack Meridian K. Hovnanian Children’s Hospital at Jersey Shore University Hospital.
Health: The Back-To-School Illnesses Doctors Say Are ‘Already On The Rise’ — And How To Tell Them Apart
These infections spread easily, he said, often through droplets created by coughing or sneezing, and can even spread when someone touches a contaminated surface and then touches their face.
Specifically, Olorunnisola said, he’s currently seeing a lot of rhinovirus infection, which is the most common cause of the cold. “Kids coming in with low-grade fevers, congestion, cough and a little bit of a sore throat,” said Olorunnisola.
Martinello added that parainfluenza virus is also widespread and “typically causes a mild self-resolving upper respiratory tract infection.”
“Also, we can see other viruses such as adenovirus,” Martinello said, which is spread by infectious respiratory particles.
Health: The Most Common Winter Viruses Doctors Are Seeing Right Now
In some folks, adenovirus can cause a cold, and in others it can progress to pneumonia. “But sometimes with certain strains of adenovirus, we see it causing more of a GI illness, and so they may have issues with diarrhea,” Martinello said.
2. COVID-19
Lots of people are testing positive for COVID-19, and that is no coincidence. “For the last two years now, we have seen a peak in the fall, and we’re definitely starting to see that now,” said Martinello.
“In particular across some of the Southeastern states, from Texas to Georgia, there is a significant amount of COVID that’s being seen,” Martinello noted, “but we’re also seeing that in other parts of the United States.”
According to Dr. Alexandra Yonts, an infectious diseases specialist at Children’s National in Washington, D.C., health department data shows an increase in COVID cases and COVID-related emergency room visits “after a relatively low disease summer.”
Health: COVID Is Spreading In These Regions Right Now — Here Are The Symptoms To Watch For
Dr. Lauren Hughes, a pediatrician and owner of Bloom Pediatrics in Kansas, added, “The most common thing I’m seeing right now is COVID. This isn’t unexpected, as we typically have a summer wave and/or back-to-school waves.”
COVID-19 symptoms often overlap with those of the common cold but with more high fever and fatigue, said Olorunnisola. Shortness of breath is also seen more in kids and adults with COVID-19.
3. Hand, foot and mouth disease
After COVID-19, Hughes said she is frequently seeing hand, foot and mouth disease.
“Hand, foot and mouth really should be renamed to hand, foot, mouth and butt because it so commonly shows up in the diaper area,” said Hughes.
Health: I'm An ER Physician. Here Are 5 Types Of Pain I'd Never Ignore.
“Usually kids will have some fussiness and low-grade fever ... they may or may not have decreased appetite or refuse to eat,” said Hughes. “Often, the rash shows up a day or two later as small dots on the soles of the feet, palms, mouth [and] diaper area.”
Hughes added that adults can also catch this virus. In grown-ups, hand, foot and mouth may appear like a cold, but can also cause painful blisters on the mouth, hands, feet and other parts of the body.
4. Flu
While flu isn’t widespread across the country, “several large pediatric centers on the West Coast have had a burst of influenza A cases over the past one to two weeks, which is abnormally early,” said Yonts.
It’s not unusual to see a “little bit of flu in October” that then goes away for a while, but the sporadic cases popping up now are early, added Martinello.

Martinello said more people are being tested for the virus now, which is likely why cases are popping up.
Flu often causes fever, body aches, chills, loss of appetite, fatigue and some general upper respiratory symptoms like congestion and cough.
5. Strep throat
Strep throat is also spreading, said Hughes. For school-age kids and older, it generally presents with the classic symptoms of sore throat, red or white spots on the tonsils, fever and painful lymph nodes, said Hughes.
“In kids 3 to 6 years old or so years, it typically does not present as throat pain, but rather as fever and abdominal pain just under their breastbone with nausea and maybe vomiting,” she said.
Strep is more prevalent in kids, but can infect adults, too. It spreads via droplets from coughing or sneezing, infected surfaces and shared food and drinks.

To avoid these illnesses, hand washing, vaccination and masking remain important.
“When it comes to prevention of COVID and other illnesses, the most useful things are the boring, unsexy ones,” said Hughes.
“If you want to avoid illness, wash your hands frequently, avoid touching your face [and] mouth without washing your hands first and mask if you are at much higher risk,” said Hughes.
A lot of these illnesses spread when someone touches an infected surface, like a doorknob or toy, and then touches their mouth or face. It’s good to teach kids to wash their hands after using the bathroom, before and after they eat, and when they get home from school, said Olorunnisola.
Some of these illnesses also spread when a sick person coughs or sneezes and spreads infected droplets. “Masks work,” said Martinello, “and they work both to protect people from these different illnesses, but also they can help to contain the germs that somebody has.”
It’s also important to prioritize the habits that can help you stay well. “Focusing on healthy lifestyle habits like sleep, exercise, nutrition and stress management can boost your immune system better than any supplement,” Mieses Malchuk said.
“The biggest onus, however, is on the sick person because we have to trust them to stay home when they are sick, cover their cough, wash their hands so they don’t pass germs on to high-touch areas,” added Hughes.
Vaccination is the best way to stay well and avoid severe disease.
Beyond daily habits, vaccination remains another key way — and the best way, said Yonts — to stay healthy this fall.
Kids and adults can get their annual flu shot, which will help protect you from severe illness and hospitalization if you do get the flu, said Yonts. The same is true for the updated COVID-19 vaccine, Yonts added.
Both shots are now available at pharmacies throughout the U.S.
The flu shot is recommended for everyone 6 months and older. The COVID-19 shot is recommended for kids 6 months to 23 months and any other child (or parent) who wants it, said Yonts.
The COVID-19 vaccine is also recommended for adults 65 and older, and for adults under 65 with an underlying condition, such as asthma, heart disease, diabetes or obesity. It’s also recommended for pregnant people.
“I cannot emphasize enough how important it is, now more than ever, especially with measles outbreaks in Virginia and Pennsylvania, that families keep their kids up to date with recommended childhood vaccines per the [American Academy of Pediatrics] schedule,” said Yonts.
If you get sick this fall, stay home until you’re better — and keep kids home from school.
If you or a loved one comes down with an illness this fall, there are a few things you should keep in mind: If you have a fever, cough, diarrhea or vomiting, stay home from work and school, said Yonts. The same goes for your child.
Olorunnisola added, “A lot of these respiratory illnesses, they tend to be mild and can be safely managed at home — just making sure your kids are resting, drinking lots of fluids and managing those fevers.”
If you notice your child is dehydrated, coughing a lot or having trouble breathing, it’s worth seeking medical attention, Olorunnisola said. If you notice these symptoms in yourself or another adult, you should also let a medical professional know.
“If symptoms persist more than 48 hours, reach out to your doctor for evaluation,” added Yonts.
Getting tested can also be helpful. If you test positive for flu or COVID, there are specific treatments available that can keep folks out of the hospital and decrease mortality, said Martinello.
“And as tempting as it is, do not rush back to school, work or exercise while recovering from illness ... it can both continue to spread the illness and can prolong your own symptoms — or in some cases (like COVID) cause new ones, like headaches, fatigue [and] nausea,” noted Yonts.
“I would like to remind parents, especially, that the goal is not really to prevent your child from ever getting sick. It’s unrealistic,” Olorunnisola said, “but the goal, really, is to prevent or reduce preventable illnesses.”
Vaccination, rest, hand washing and masking are all great ways to stay well.

Title: CNNs Goldberg Says Macklemore Ban Not Censorship Criticizes Israel Coverage
Article_Text:
Two weeks ago the opening act for Ed Sheeran's concert at MetLife Stadium, Macklemore, called for a "Free Palestine", and did his anti-Israel song, "Hind's Hall," resulting in him being dropped form Sheeran's tour. The story has fascinated the leftist media. On Tuesday, ABC's World News Tonight led with it over a thwarted terror attack in Pennsylvania, and Thursday on CNN's The Arena, Jonah Goldberg ripped the media's obsession with the story.
Host Kasie Hunt led the segment with a clip of Macklemore's remarks.
HUNT: Those comments from Macklemore have become a flashpoint in the conversation over the support for Palestinian people and free speech.... Macklemore has since been dropped from the tour ahead of scheduled performances in Boston. New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft saying that Macklemore would be unwelcome to perform at the stadium. All of Sheeran's other supporting acts then quit the tour in a show of solidarity with Macklemore. On Wednesday, Macklemore announced he would donate all the money he made on the tour to organizations supporting Palestinians, and he invited raft to match it. Kraft said he already committed to donate $2 million to aid in the region.
Hunt left out that reportedly Macklemore's $1 million donation went to six aid groups supporting Palestinians, including three with Hamas and other terrorist ties. She also ignored that in 2014 he came on stage dressed in a Jewish caricature costume. That information wouldn't fit in with the next clip she played.
MACKLEMORE: To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace. Love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality. So I say free Palestine. I say free Lebanon. I say free Cuba. I say free Congo, free Sudan.
He then added, "Free all people in America living in fear over this terrorist organization ICE," but of course Hunt made no mention of it. Instead she turned to CNN entertainment reporter Lisa France and asked her to explain "how we got here." France proceeded to give a most sympathetic report on Macklemore's situation.
Hunt followed France's report with a clip of Fox News's Jesse Watters saying that he doesn't think "free Palestine" is hate speech, and she asked Goldberg what he thought, and he unloaded.
GOLDBERG: The use of censorship in this whole thing is ridiculous. Robert Kraft has free speech rights, too. It's his venue. He has every right as a private citizen who owns the venue to say, there's certain things I don't want in my venue. Second of all, I think Macklemore, I'm sure his heart's in the right place, is basically a virtue signaling cliche generator. And while I agree the criticism of Israel, I have criticisms of Israel, is not necessarily anti-Semitic, but the disproportionate, wildly disproportionate in terms of media coverage, Israel is more covered as a country than like the next 20 countries combined. That can't be explained solely because of what's going on in Palestine.
Not when, China, which actually is an apartheid state, they practice Han supremacy there. They are destroying Tibet. They're destroying the Uyghurs in putting the Uyghurs, millions of Uyghurs in concentration camps. But people want to talk about apartheid in Israel, even though Arab Israelis have full voting rights and are represented in the Knesset, it starts to fee like a selective prosecution in a lot of ways to me.
This kind of thing is very faddish, pumped out a lot on social media, and I don't have a huge amount of patience for it.... I also don't think genocide is happening in Israel, in Gaza.
Goldberg then hit the nail on the head on Macklemore.
GOLDBERG: I'm just also exhausted by this argument that comes up every 15 minutes in our culture about artists thinking that they have this special place in our culture to give their opinions, often uninformed, not just on this, but on plenty of things. They use their status as a platform every year at the Oscars, someone gets an award and then pees from a great height on people that everyone in the room also dislikes, and everyone salutes their bravery for saying things that they're only going to get applause for. It's a boring argument. It happens all the time and like nothing new can be said about the fundamental issues about free speech and all this because government has nothing to do with censoring anybody.
Goldberg covered the absurdity of this story from all angles, and was unafraid. This is CNN?

Title: Vot-ER wants voters to connect health care, civic engagement
Article_Text:
Campaign to combine health care advocacy with civic engagement and voting comes to Philadelphia’s Point Breeze neighborhood
Young people face health care decisions shaped by policy. Vot-ER is working to connect health care experiences with civic engagement and voting.
What questions do you have about the 2026 elections? What major issues do you want candidates to address? Let us know.
Young people consistently cite affordability and health care among the issues that shape their political views and voting decisions. But where do health care and civic engagement overlap in their day to day lives?
That’s the question Vot-ER is trying to bring into hospitals and doctors offices around the nation, where health care professionals are increasingly becoming messengers for civic engagement.
The nonpartisan organization founded by Dr. Alister Martin, New York City’s health commissioner, to integrate civic engagement into health care equips medical professionals with voter registration assistance and election reminders to pass onto patients. This includes specialized badges that allow eligible patients to register to vote, request a mail ballot or learn about upcoming elections on the platform.
On Tuesday, the organization set up a table in Philadelphia’s Point Breeze neighborhood to encourage residents to register to vote and learn more about Vot-ER.
The link between health care and policy can be easy to miss
For Jeff Mathwig, the connection between health and civic participation was made clear on the campaign trail. When working on Al Franken’s campaign for the U.S. Senate, he met a voter who was unable to leave her house due to severe back pain. After speaking with her for an hour about health policies, he was able to see the “intersection between health care and civic engagement.”
Today, Mathwig is the civic health fellow at Vot-ER where he wants young people to understand that legislation will impact them, especially their health care experiences.
“There’s always a group of people that are really engaged, and those are the people that you typically see in the news. But a lot of times young people, they’re just not as engaged,” he said. “So how do you get them more involved? You [have] to make them understand how this is going to impact them in the future.”
Adam Bilodeau, a public health nurse at the National Nurse Led Care Consortium, said that health care is heavily impacted by “who is making certain policies and who’s regulating those policies. And I think folks are a little bit removed from that.”
The Affordable Care Act allows young people to remain on their parents’ health insurance coverage until they turn 26 and Bilodeau notes that this may be part of the reason some young people are not thinking about health care when they vote.
However, Anthony Rumbos-Perez, a 22-year-old who works as a public benefits paralegal at AIDS Law Project of Pennsylvania, said “not every child has the privilege of having parents who are employed and have good health insurance coverage.”
For Rumbos-Perez, navigating the health care system has made the connection between policy and everyday life difficult to ignore.
“The system is built to not be easily understandable. It’s all incredibly difficult to navigate if you’re already dealing with the stress of being low income and the fear of losing health insurance,” he said.
Integrating voter education in health care offices
When you go to a doctor’s office, the intake form traditionally asks you to disclose if you drink, smoke, wear a seat belt, are sexually active and if you exercise. For Mallory Stanek, the Pennsylvania organizing manager at Vot-ER, civics can be integrated in a health care setting through the addition of one simple question: Are you registered to vote?
“It’s just that simple,” she said.
The American Medical Association adopted a policy in 2022 recognizing voting as a social determinant of health. Data from the Health & Democracy Index found that states with higher voter turnout and civic engagement have better health outcomes. Stanek said that states can increase civic participation by simply bringing civic resources into hospitals and doctors’ offices.
“If they’re never being asked anywhere else, then they’re probably not going to vote or know anything about it … Bringing these resources into the hospitals, having posters when you walk into waiting rooms,” she said, adding that could eliminate “the stigma and a lot of the barriers around voting and accessing that information.”
Anna Koopman is a public health nurse home visitor at the National Nurse-Led Care Consortium and offered information at a table alongside Vot-ER on Tuesday. When asked whether people have told her that voting education is “not a health care provider’s job,” she pointed to the broader role of health care in promoting well-being and empowering people to make decisions for themselves.
“It’s about [promoting] better health. It’s about empowering folks to be able to make decisions for themselves, to have autonomy,” she said.
In order to engage young people and increase voter education, Vot-ER connects with pediatric providers to ensure that young people are equipped with simple, straightforward information about how to register to vote and where to find information about elections. In addition, providers can ensure students who are getting ready to go to college know that they can register to vote at their college address, Stanek noted.
What health care means to young voters
Bianca Little teaches a course called “peace and social change” for high school seniors. As a teacher, she said it is important that her pupils receive well-rounded civics education in order to “help them become critical thinkers, especially in [the] climate that we have right now, politically and socially, where there’s so much misinformation.”
She added that a civics education is undeniably tied to health care as it involves “understanding how to take care of yourself. If you’re gonna take care of your community, you have to have that foundation within yourself first.”
Many of her students have a strong understanding of the connection between health care and civics as they have experiences with family members who are sick or living with a disability and have encountered difficulties with accessibility services.
“All of these things are connected because I think civics teaches you when you see something wrong, how do you start to fix it? I think we live in a society that isn’t fully aware and cognizant of people who are disabled or people who aren’t able bodied. So the two are married,” Little said.
Sarah Weill-Jones, a disability justice advocate from Philadelphia, is currently on their mother’s insurance but is becoming increasingly worried about what they will do once they turn 26.
“Who knows what job I’ll have? Who knows what schooling I’ll be in during that time, and if I’ll have a job that gives me the benefits that I’ll need to access the same level of health care that I’m receiving now?” they said.
For them, health care is a priority when deciding how to vote.
“If your representative is not actively advocating for you to receive quality health care and providers that are invested in your well-being, then it’s not someone that you should be voting for,” they said.
Weill-Jones said that Vot-ER’s initiative to increase voter and civic education by integrating it with health care is “absolutely a no brainer.” However, they also believe that these civic projects should expand beyond doctors offices as many voters may not have the coverage required to see a provider.
In terms of public policy, Rumbos-Perez said that “Medicare for All” has been a “rallying cry for a lot of young people”. The proposed bill would establish a universal single-payer national health insurance system.
Many young people become deeply aware of the link between health care and civics “the second that you yourself are dealing with the bureaucracy of either private medical insurance or public health care,” Rumbos-Perez said.
“I hold on to the hope that in my lifetime we will pass something like ‘Medicare for All’ in the U.S., but that takes people to be civically engaged and to use whatever political voice they have to make that happen,” he said.

Title: Ed Sheeran returns to stage after Macklemore was removed and other acts withdrew over Palestine row
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran is set to return to the stage in Philadelphia on Saturday, 19 September, for the first time since a dispute over Macklemore's removal from his Loop tour led all of his remaining supporting acts to withdraw. The singer is scheduled to perform at Lincoln Financial Field, with no replacement opening act announced. His return comes after a turbulent week in which his US tour was reshaped by a dispute involving Macklemore's comments about the Israel-Gaza conflict and the decision to remove him from the remaining dates. Macklemore had been performing as an opening act for Sheeran's US shows. During his performances at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey in early September, the rapper spoke about Gaza and the occupied West Bank and said "Free Palestine". He also performed his protest song Hind's Hall, which he released in 2024 in solidarity with Palestinians. The comments were followed by calls for Macklemore to be removed from the tour. The Israeli-American Council had launched a petition seeking his removal, while venue owners also raised objections. Reuters reported that the tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, said venue owners had refused to host shows with Macklemore on the bill. Sheeran subsequently addressed the controversy, saying the decision to remove Macklemore had been made by the promoter and venues rather than him. He said he had been involved in discussions with promoters and venues in an attempt to find a resolution, but that the decision was ultimately final. He also said he had personal views on the conflict but had chosen not to discuss them publicly. Finneas, who was due to support Sheeran on six South American dates in November, announced that he was withdrawing from the tour. In a statement shared on social media, he said artists should not be silenced when speaking about people they believe are oppressed and said he stood with Palestine and its people. Irish singer Aaron Rowe also pulled out of the remaining North American dates. He said the decision was difficult because of his relationship with Sheeran, but that he could not continue with the tour amid the circumstances surrounding Macklemore's removal. Danish group Lukas Graham followed, while Beoga, the Irish band that had been performing alongside Sheeran during parts of his set, also withdrew. That leaves Sheeran facing his Philadelphia performance without the supporting acts who had been part of the tour's recent US dates. The singer already performs much of the Loop show alone, although Beoga had joined him for several songs. According to The Independent, his website had not listed a replacement act ahead of Saturday's concert. The Philadelphia show is also expected to take place amid continued demonstrations linked to the controversy. Pro-Palestinian groups have announced plans to protest outside Lincoln Financial Field, keeping the dispute over Macklemore's removal in public view as Sheeran resumes the tour. Macklemore has since announced that he will donate $1 million from his tour earnings to Palestinian relief efforts and challenged New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft to match the donation. Kraft and Sheeran have reportedly agreed to contribute $2 million collectively, although details about where that money will be directed have not been specified. Sheeran's Loop tour is scheduled to continue after Philadelphia, with further North American and South American dates before its planned conclusion in Mexico City in December.
